name: Cloudways
summary: Managed-hosting layer that rents you servers on DigitalOcean, Vultr, Linode, AWS or Google Cloud through one dashboard, with the stack, caching, staging, cloning, backups and 24/7 platform support pre-built on top. You buy a server and put as many sites on it as it holds — no per-site plans and no visit metering — billed hourly and invoiced monthly in arrears with no contract. The trade is control: Cloudways' own documentation states there is no root access and no bring-your-own cloud account, so the server lives in Cloudways' name. Owned by DigitalOcean since September 2022.
best_for: agencies and PHP shops running many sites who want servers managed but not metered. One server holds as many sites as it can carry with no visit caps, billing is hourly and post-paid with no annual term, and Magento and Laravel are first-class alongside WordPress. It suits teams who genuinely do not want anyone patching kernels at 2am
skip_if: you are comfortable in a terminal, or you run a single small site. Going direct to the cloud provider with your own control panel keeps the server in your own account for materially less. And one low-traffic site is better served by shared hosting, or by a per-site managed host that bundles CDN and application support. Cloudways also has no email hosting of its own, reselling a Rackspace add-on instead
honest_knock: "Fully managed" here means the server, not your site — and that distinction is where the money is. Cloudways' own support page puts infrastructure and platform work in the included tier but treats application help as guidance only. Plugin and theme troubleshooting, database work and performance tuning sit behind Advanced Support at $100/month or 10% of your invoice, whichever is higher, on a six-month minimum. On a small server that add-on costs more than the server it supports. Content changes, custom code debugging and code audits stay out of scope on every tier, paid ones included. The deeper catch is ownership: Cloudways documents that you get no root access and cannot use your own cloud credentials, so the machine sits in Cloudways' account — you cannot fire the management layer and keep the server, you migrate. And read the billing terms before you rely on it: their help centre states that an unpaid invoice restricts server access and can lead to the server and its backups being deleted, with backups kept for only 14 days after deletion.

pricing.plans_source: hand-curated from the vendor's pricing page
pricing.notes: (read 2026-08-26 on cloudways.com/en/pricing.php, DigitalOcean tab) No free tier, but a 3-day free trial with no credit card required. Billing is hourly and post-paid, invoiced in the first week of the following month, with no annual contract — and the hourly figure is the one that decides the bill: every card divides its monthly price by 672 hours, so $0.0208 an hour is the $14 plan. The page now opens on DigitalOcean's Premium (NVMe) column, where Micro is 1GB RAM / 1 vCPU / 25GB NVMe / 1TB bandwidth at $14/month, Small 2GB / 1 vCPU / 50GB NVMe / 2TB at $28, Medium 4GB / 2 vCPU / 80GB / 4TB at $54 and Large 8GB / 4 vCPU / 160GB / 5TB at $99. Two of those have moved since July: the entry machine is now half the size for three dollars more (July's Micro was 2GB / 50GB at $11), and the 8GB plan went from $88 to $99. Switch the column to Standard and that same 2GB / 50GB box reads $11 a month — but the hourly figure printed underneath it, $0.0357, works out to $24 at the 672-hour month the other cards use, so the two numbers on that one card cannot both be right; read the live estimate before you commit. Bought direct from DigitalOcean on the same day, an 8GB / 4 vCPU / 160GB / 5TB droplet lists at $0.07143 an hour, $48 a month. Add-ons are monthly and separate: Cloudflare Enterprise CDN from $4.99 per domain, Site Manager from $3 per app, Malware Protection from $4 per app, Rackspace email $1 per mailbox, DNS Made Easy $0.50 per domain, offsite backup storage $0.033 per GB. Advance Support is $100/month or 10% of your invoice, whichever is higher, with a limited-time flat rate of $25/month advertised on the page today; the $500 Premium Support tier we recorded in July is no longer listed there. Cloudways Autonomous, the separate autoscaling product, now prices at $35, $240 and $995 a month where July's page showed $99, $199 and $399, and it meters unique visits and bandwidth rather than RAM (30k visits and 100GB on Small, 70k and 200GB on Medium) with a 3-day free trial. Markups on AWS and Google Cloud still cannot be calculated because Cloudways does not publish the underlying instance types. A site-wide banner advertises 40% off for four months until 15 September 2026 — promotions move, so read the live price. US list prices, excluding tax. Re-verified 12 October 2026 in a live browser on cloudways.com/en/pricing.php: Micro $14 ($0.0208 an hour), Small $28 ($0.0417), Medium $54 ($0.0804) and Large $99 ($0.1473) on the DigitalOcean Premium column, unchanged; the page adds $0.033/GB per server for offsite backup storage and says listed prices exclude taxes. The support page still lists Advanced at $100 a month or 10% of the invoice, whichever is higher, and Premium at $500 on the same rule, next to a banner offering Advanced at '$25/mo flat' as a 'Lifetime deal: 75% OFF'.

compare_with.name: Going direct on DigitalOcean with your own control panel
compare_with.why: DigitalOcean owns Cloudways and sells both sides, which makes this the honest comparison: the same 8GB machine is $48/month as a droplet and $99/month wrapped in Cloudways. Add DigitalOcean's own daily backups and a control-panel licence and a like-for-like self-managed box lands nearer $75-80, so the real premium is smaller than the sticker gap suggests. The decisive difference is not price but ownership: with your own droplet the account and root are yours and you can drop the panel and keep the server, whereas leaving Cloudways is a migration

sessions.what: Tested by our team on 25 October 2026 on the 3-day Flexible trial: Daan created and verified the account and our AI assistant ran the test in Daan's browser. We launched a DigitalOcean server with WordPress, imported two made-up rows into a separate database table, exported them as SQL and updated one of them.
findings: The Flexible trial needed no card before launch. The setup screen showed DigitalOcean Premium 4GB at $54.00 a month ($0.0804 an hour) and $0 during the trial, with billing starting only when the account is upgraded. The server took about nine minutes to provision.

In Database Manager we imported our test rows into a table of their own (4 successful queries). Text, Unicode, dates, exact decimal amounts, a true/false field (stored as tinyint) and an empty value kept apart from NULL all came through; the attachment column holds only a file path.

Exporting just that table as SQL returned both rows with their native IDs 1 and 2 next to our own IDs. We then ran an SQL UPDATE on the native key (2 successful queries): only the second row's text changed and no duplicates appeared. This is a database update, not an import screen in the app.

Adding a payment method to upgrade opens the card form before any final plan total. The form mentions a $1 verification that is reversed after authorization, and the page said 'Taxes Do not Apply to your current invoice based on your account information.' We entered no card.

Our three support questions in the chat were answered within seconds by Cloudways' AI agent: it described a full application backup you can download over SFTP, said Copilot may share server and application logs with OpenAI-based models, and passed the DPA question to a human agent. We saw no human reply in that session.
not_tested: A full application backup or a restore into an empty server
Uploading media or other binary files
Cancelling or deleting the server and account
sessions.note: Findings as written up after the session; no pass/fail per task was scored.
